articles.title: Whom Did God Give Land
articles.author: Paul deLespinasse
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Disputes over land have long riled the human race. A popular argument has been that a particular group was given rights to land by God. Numerous passages in Genesis, the first book of the Bible’s Old Testament, assert that God gave particular lands forever to the people now referred to as Israelis. In Exodus 3:7-8 we are told: “And the LORD said, I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt, and have heard their cry by reason of their taskmasters; for I know their sorrows; “And I am come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians, and to bring them up out of that land unto a good land and a large, unto a land flowing with milk and honey; unto the place of the Canaanites, and the Hittites, and the Amorites, and the Perizzites, and the Hivites, and the Jebusites.” Interestingly, there were already people (the Canaanites, and others) living in this promised land. If God was giving this land to the Israelis, did this mean that it was exclusively theirs, or that they would be its privileged class? What about the Canaanites and other groups already living there? Could they be expelled? Were they not equally children of God? This is not merely an historical question. This issue still comes up today. In Israel substantial numbers of people think that God’s alleged donation gives them exclusive rights to occupy the area, and that other people can legitimately be killed or forced to leave. Similar attitudes exist among many Palestinians, who descend from people already living in the area when holocaust survivors moved there after World War II. Their controversial slogan “From the river to the sea, Palestine will be free” refers to all of the territory between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea including all of present day Israel. Related: Bombers or Solar Panels? The Real Cost of America's Military Priorities The issue is also with us in other parts of today’s world. Various indigenous peoples movements claim that their rights based on priority were violated by all the illegal European aliens moving into the Americas and Australia. In various circles today Land Acknowledgments apologize for this “injustice.” In the United States today there are also people who believe that descendants of their European ancestors who arrived in the past have the right to make it illegal for new people to move in. In effect, they too are claiming a God-given right to exclusive residency. It seems to me that the Bible, written by human beings and reflecting human views, can sometimes get things wrong, and that the claim that God gave territory exclusively to the descendants of Abraham was just plain wrong. Why would a just God do any such thing? The writers may have allowed their political interests to override any actual messages they were receiving from on high. As Thomas Hobbes noted in his Leviathon (1651), “If Livy say the Gods once made a cow speak, and we believe him not, we distrust not God therein, but Livy.” The Russian Orthodox church may have a good idea here. My Russian Bible calls the New Testament the Новый Завет (Novy Zavet), using the standard Russian term for “new.” But it calls what we call the Old Testament the Вехтий Завет (Bekty Zavet), not using Старый (starry) , the usual Russian term for “old.” I had to look the new term up, and it translates as “ decrepit ” or “ worn out .” “Worn out” may be too strong for the Old Testament in general, but it could be about right for its discussion of land grants. This religious belief has had terrible consequences throughout human history. Related: The Impossible Will Take a Little While: The Power of Persistence Let’s assume there is a just God who created the universe and everything in it. It makes more sense to conclude that land is given, not to particular groups of people, but to the human race in general. If this is true, it means that indigenous peoples who occupy territory have no natural right to exclude other people from moving in. (However, it does not excuse the atrocious behavior of the new settlers towards the people already living there.) It also means that today’s Americans have no natural right to exclude other people from moving in, to treat them very shabbily, and to force many of them to go somewhere else. It has been human beings, not God, who divided the world up into separate territories. It is up to us to correct this mistake.

articles.title: Major Jason Watson
articles.author: Jeffrey Sterling
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. For almost two months, an Air Force officer has been sitting alone in a cell, twenty-four hours a day. When they let him out to eat or exercise, he’s still alone, according to his attorney . His name is Major Jason Watson. He hasn’t been convicted of anything. Under military law he is presumed innocent, yet he’s still in that cell. I know something about solitary confinement. I also know what it feels like when a government would rather silence you than answer for its transgressions. That’s why I can’t stay quiet about Major Watson. And it’s why I think we need to talk about the kind of courage this country says it admires, right up until someone actually shows it. What Major Watson Did On July 1, Major Watson walked up the House steps of the U.S. Capitol in uniform and stood there holding a sign that read “Impeach. Convict. Remove.” He was calling for the removal of President Trump and Vice President Vance. Capitol Police arrested him . The D.C. charges were dropped, but he was taken from the courthouse straight into Air Force custody and restricted to base . In August he went on CNN and said it again. The next day, the Air Force ordered him into pretrial confinement . He now faces ten charges under three articles of the Uniform Code of Military Justice (UCMJ): three under Article 88 for allegedly using “contemptuous words” against the president, five under Article 92 for failing to obey orders or regulations, and two under Article 133 for “conduct unbecoming an officer,” as his lawyers confirmed in a public statement . I’m not here to argue about uniform regulations. What bothers me, and what should bother anyone paying attention, is what the Article 88 charges and that solitary cell tell us about how power handles real dissent.Watson didn’t hide behind a fake name. He didn’t retain or leak anything classified. He put his own name and face on what he believed, in public, knowing what it would cost. Before he took that stand, he asked himself, “What’s the highest price that I’m willing to pay?” His answer was, more or less, whatever it takes. That’s what bravery looks like. You’re still afraid. You go anyway, knowing hell is coming. Related: Major Jason Watson, Trump, and the Military’s Duty to Defy Illegal Orders Punished Before He Is Tried Here is what troubles me most. The military is punishing Major Watson while claiming to follow the very rules that forbid it. Article 13 of the UCMJ says no one being held for trial may be punished, and that pretrial confinement may be no “more rigorous than the circumstances require to insure his presence.” The idea is straight-forward. Someone waiting for a court-martial is presumed innocent, and the military isn’t allowed to treat him as guilty. Locking a person alone in a cell for months is punishment by any ordinary meaning of the word. Watson’s attorney has said solitary is usually reserved for people who are violent or disobedient, and even then only for a few days or a week. At Watson’s Article 32 hearing, the hearing officer said the isolation was required because he can’t be housed with civilian inmates. Even if you accept that explanation, it doesn’t undo what isolation does to a person’s mind. And it doesn’t answer the bigger question: why is a peaceful man whose only “offense” was speaking locked up at all? You can’t even argue that the punishment doesn’t fit the crime, because officially it isn’t punishment. When the people offended by your words also get to decide what counts as a crime, and what counts as punishment, the law stops being fair or predictable. I can tell you from experience that solitary is built to grind you down. I was thrown into solitary in prison because I wouldn’t let a guard on a power trip treat me as anything less than a human being. My punishment for standing up for my dignity was a cell less than half the size of my usual cage. No window. No sunlight. Nothing to remind me there was a world outside. No contact with anyone, including my family, who went days without hearing from me and had no idea what was happening. That kind of isolation isn’t about safety or order or paperwork. It’s about breaking someone, and about sending a message to everyone else. Major Watson stood up against an administration he believes is trampling the Constitution. For that act of conscience, they’re trying to make him disappear. Article 88 and the Espionage Act Article 88 makes it a crime for a commissioned officer to use “contemptuous words” against the president, the vice president, Congress, and certain other officials. It is almost never used. A CNN review found only two convictions under it since the modern military code took effect in 1950. The military’s own Manual for Courts-Martial, as one legal analysis explains , says that criticism of an official in the course of political discussion, even strongly worded criticism, shouldn’t be charged under this article unless it is personally contemptuous. Watson put it simply at his hearing : “discomfort is not contempt.” How the article gets used is concerning. In 2021, Marine Lt. Col. Stuart Scheller posted videos in uniform demanding accountability from senior leaders over the Afghanistan withdrawal, at one point saying he felt “contempt” for them. He was charged under Article 88 too. With prominent supporters cheering him on, his case went to a special court-martial, the lower-level forum. He spent nine days in the brig, pleaded guilty, and walked away with a letter of reprimand and a $5,000 forfeiture of pay . Watson’s lawyers summed up the problem : “The law will not make the same word a virtue in one officer’s mouth and a felony in another’s.” I recognize this double standard because I’ve lived it. The Espionage Act of 1917 was written to catch spies. Today it’s regularly used against whistleblowers who tell the public what the government would rather keep quiet, and defendants usually aren’t allowed to argue that their disclosures served the public interest. Groups like PEN America, the ACLU, and Human Rights Watch have warned for years that laws this broad invite selective prosecution. The cases of John Kiriakou, Reality Winner, and Thomas Drake show those warnings were right. Look at Courtney Williams, who worked in a support role for Delta Force at Fort Bragg from 2010 to 2016. She talked to an investigative reporter about sexual harassment and discrimination inside the unit. In April, the FBI arrested her , and she now faces four Espionage Act counts , each carrying up to ten years. Prosecutors say some of what she shared was classified. The reporter she spoke with calls the case retaliation against a whistleblower. Either way, plenty of former special operators talk openly about their units on popular podcasts without ending up in handcuffs. Article 88 and the Espionage Act are different laws, but they end up doing the same job. They’re old, broad nets that can be thrown over anyone who speaks uncomfortable truths about those in power. Whether the target is a whistleblower or an outspoken officer, the result is silence. And every time we let these tools get dusted off, we make it easier to use them on the next person. The Oath Wasn’t to a Person Every public servant, civilian or military, swears to support and defend the Constitution. None of them swears loyalty to a president, a party, or a movement. There’s a difference between the enlisted and officer oaths worth knowing. Enlisted members promise to “obey the orders of the President of the United States and the orders of the officers appointed over me.” Officers don’t make that promise. Under the officer’s oath , they swear to support and defend the Constitution and to “well and faithfully discharge the duties” of their office. That difference, as the Marine Corps itself explains , is deliberate. An officer’s final loyalty belongs to the Constitution and the rule of law, not to whoever is sitting in the Oval Office. Watson has said his oath is exactly why he went to those Capitol steps, and that he acted out of duty, not partisanship. His point is that no leader is above the law. Yet “support and defend the Constitution” keeps getting bent into a demand for personal loyalty. People who stand on principle end up in solitary. People who look the other way get promoted. Service and Speech I have deep respect for the military and its traditions. The military can’t be anyone’s political tool, and service members have to follow lawful orders. The rules that keep uniforms out of partisan politics exist for good reason: they keep the military under civilian control and out of the hands of any one side. Those rules matter. But this is about proportion. Joining the military doesn’t mean giving up your basic rights. Courts have long held that service members keep some free-speech protection, even if it is narrower than a civilian’s, as long as their speech doesn’t seriously threaten discipline or the mission. So it’s fair to ask where the line really is. Does one peaceful protest justify criminal charges and months in solitary? A military confident enough to handle criticism from within its own ranks is stronger than one that keeps people in line through fear. “I Was Only Following Orders” We settled the question of blind obedience after World War II. At Nuremberg, the world rejected “just following orders” as an excuse. The principle that came out of those trials says acting on orders doesn’t relieve you of responsibility “provided a moral choice was in fact possible.” Our own military law requires service members to obey lawful orders, not unlawful ones. We rightly honor people like Hugh Thompson, the Army helicopter pilot who landed his aircraft between American soldiers and fleeing Vietnamese civilians at My Lai in 1968. He was treated as an outcast for years. The Army didn’t award him the Soldier’s Medal until 1998, thirty years later. We can’t keep telling every generation of service members that they have a duty to refuse wrongdoing, then crush the ones who actually say so out loud. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. wrote about this from a Birmingham jail cell . We have a duty to obey just laws, he said, and an equal duty to disobey unjust ones. But “one who breaks an unjust law must do so openly, lovingly, and with a willingness to accept the penalty.” That’s the tradition Major Watson acted in. He didn’t hide. He stood in the open, told his superiors where he stood, and accepted the consequences. If the right of conscience doesn’t belong to every citizen, it doesn’t really belong to anyone. And a country where no one can tell the powerful the truth isn’t a free country. What We Owe Him Major Watson has shown a steady, stubborn courage that’s rare anywhere, and rarer still when your career and freedom are on the line. He didn’t hide behind technicalities or double-talk. He put everything on the line for the principles he swore to uphold. We owe him our voices, for his sake and for our own. When the government turns its full weight against someone who takes his oath seriously, we can’t just wait for politicians or courts to fix it. It takes ordinary people, standing together, to demand fairness, shine a light into those cells, and make sure the people who tell the truth don’t have to stand alone. I encourage everyone to show support for Major Watson by spreading the word about his courage and how he is being persecuted for standing up for truth. You can also help by sending letters of support to Major Watson while he is being confined to the following address: Jason P. Watson Calvert County Detention Center P.O. Box 9 Barstow, MD 20610

articles.title: New World Crimes
articles.author: Peter Laarman
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Subjugation, domination, exploitation, extraction: it no longer strikes anyone as odd to associate these behaviors with Americans who are eager to call themselves Christians. But many observers also think of this excrescence as a new development in Christianity. If only!! Those with some grasp of the backstory can find a discernable line of descent from the English Puritans, a self-described “chosen” people who took it upon themselves to purify the Protestant project, ridding it of all popish residues. They began as dissenters in England only to end as theocrats here, crushing all dissent in governing their settlements in Connecticut and Massachusetts. They also took it upon themselves to dispossess, enslave, and murder Indigenous people here as part of “The Glorious Works of Christ in America” (the name given to the project by Puritan divine Increase Mather). This was happening while their Puritan counterpart back in the Mother Country—the Lord Protector, Oliver Cromwell—was colonizing Ireland in the name of safeguarding Protestantism from possible Catholic subversion. Twenty percent of Ireland’s population is believed to have died in this subjugation process. As I say, much of this is now well known. What fewer people pay attention to is what happened in late 15 th century Spain, before there was even such a thing as Protestantism. Not to give the killer Protestants a pass, but it would be hard to beat the Spain of Ferdinand and Isabella in respect to intolerance, cruelty, and ethnic cleansing dressed up as piety. Wanting to know more about Spain, I was glad to come across a tightly written and well-researched account of the convergence of reconquest, purification, and colonization by Their Most Holy Catholic Majesties, Ferdinand and Isabella. The book, by James Reston, Jr., is titled Dogs of God: Columbus, the Inquisition, and the Defeat of the Moors. “Dogs of God” was a label proudly worn by friars of the Dominican order, founded in the 13 th during the Church’s fraught effort to put down heretics in southern France. In Ferdinand and Isabella’s time, these tough Dominicans became central figures in the Spanish Inquisition, a campaign created to purge a united Spanish kingdom of all doctrinal impurity while consolidating royal power. The campaign was primarily focused on Christians suspected of having Jewish blood. The first Grand Inquisitor—the much-feared Torquemada , notorious for his brutal methods—was a Dominican. His agents “relaxed” (tortured) suspected heretics to get confessions, then burned them in spectacular displays called Acts of Faith . Licensed by the pope, the Inquisition’s reign of terror under Ferdinand and Isabella was complemented by these monarchs’ creation of a national police force to undermine the authority of regional nobles, widespread confiscations of nobles’ properties, imposition of a national currency, and unification by means of Castilian as a national language. All of this was suffused in lavish displays of piety. Isabella, a beautiful and brilliant leader, was especially deft at inviting comparisons of herself to the Virgin Mary, orchestrating gorgeous triumphal processions, and building shrines wherever she went. With a charismatic partner like this, a grim and tightlipped Ferdinand could focus on liquidating rivals and planning the military conquest of Moorish territory in the south. Fun fact: Niccolo Machiavelli modeled his cunning Prince on the calculating, ruthless Ferdinand. Related: Beyond Plantation Capitalism: Rev. Peter Laarman on the Fight for Economic Justice The First New World Conquistador: Columbus as Religious Zealot It is widely known that Columbus was an Italian sailor of humble origins who washed up in Spain looking for opportunity. He was also a mystic who was enthralled by the idea that he might not just find the riches of the East by sailing West: he might also somehow effectuate the reconquest of the Holy Land by Christians. Realizing how susceptible the pious Isabella was to this sort of jive, he eventually won her patronage by dangling Holy Jerusalem in front of her own crusading ambition. Reston vividly imagines the pitch made by a fame-hungry Genoese mariner to a receptive queen in 1489, on the eve of the final subjugation of the Moors in Granada and the subsequent expulsion of all unbaptized Jews from Catholic Spain: Discovery must join Reconquest and Purification. Together, the three fitted into the new heaven and the new earth that was promised in the Book of Revelation. Ferdinand, Torquemada, and Columbus were to be the queen’s—and God’s—instruments in a passion play. Columbus even promised the queen that if she would bankroll and bless his western adventure, he would contribute the profits to fund a glorious new crusade in the Holy Land. The monarchs weren’t ready to act just then, in 1489. They had other things on their mind. But in the flush of victory against Muslims in the south two years later—a central goal of Christian Europe for 800 years—and just as they were imposing their final solution upon a long-established Jewish population, the sovereigns finally gave Columbus the green light. Before casting off, he painted the sails of his little caravels with the Crusaders’ cross—the same square cross used by the Knights Templar. Enroute to his port of departure, Columbus encountered Jews fleeing for their lives: two nightmares unfolded at the very same moment. Related: Marlon James Uncovers Depths of Depravity in Evangelical Christianity Imperial Rivalry, Colonization, and Slavery By now, many people also know that New World colonization received the Church’s seal of approval by way of a papal bull (two bulls, actually) issued in 1493. This is the origin of the so-called Doctrine of Discovery . But there is more to know, and Reston supplies vital details. Ferdinand and Isabella were seriously haunted by the fear that rival Portugal might beat them to the punch in New World conquests. After all, Portuguese navigators were widely recognized to be the best in the world: they had sailed around the Cape of Good Hope, they had already established colonies in Africa, and they were on their way to colonizing India and capturing Asia’s lucrative spice market. Spain also knew their rival was aware that Columbus had found something very interesting on his first voyage: the admiral’s storm-wracked Nina had actually been forced to dock in Portugal before finally limping into Spanish waters. In view of this threat, Spain demanded that a Spanish pope (a splendidly debauched Alexander VI—Rodrigo Borgia by birth) grant them secure protection for the lands Columbus had “discovered.” So yes, Rome’s sanction for conquest was important, but ultimately more important was Spain’s direct negotiation with Portugal to divide up the globe. Intense negotiation led to a treaty in 1494, and in this treaty, Spain came up short. Portugal’s negotiators managed to re-draw the pope’s dividing line hundreds of miles to the west, with a major unanticipated bonus for Lisbon. In 1500, the Portuguese realized just what a sweet deal they had made when a fleet bound for India bumped into Brazil while taking an extreme western course in order to avoid navigation troubles closer to Africa. Not only could they keep all their rich possessions in Africa and India, but now they also had access to a vast lowland terrain ideal for growing sugar cane. As the Portuguese were already well into African slavery, and as they had already figured out how to grow and process cane sugar by way of their Eastern connections, they could and did put two and two together to start building a lucrative slavery-based sugar economy. Between 1501 and 1875, tiny Portugal would transport half of all the Africans delivered into New World bondage: some six million people in all. The Spaniards brutally enslaved people for the purpose of extracting precious metals; the Portuguese enslaved far more people in order to extract sugar from endless fields of cane. By the time the growing Dutch and British empires came along to horn in on Portugal’s sugar bonanza in the mid-17 th century, the New World’s sugar would be proving far more valuable than its silver and gold. Related: Curbing Cancerous Capitalism: An Organizing Challenge for the Ages White Christian Supremacy at the Dawn of Modernity All this backdrop may seem beside the point when thinking about today’s white Christian nationalism, but in fact it is highly relevant to understanding the incubation of a toxic strain. Although Ferdinand and Isabella initially rebuked Columbus for enslaving Indigenous Caribbeans (his second expedition was a wild festival of plunder), it was soon obvious to all Europeans that what they faced in the New World would be a labor shortage of staggering proportions, given the amount of land and resources available for exploitation. Enslaving the natives would never be sufficient; deploying indentured white labor wouldn’t cut it; African slavery emerged as the solution. The Christians even believed their anti-Black racism had a biblical warrant in the so-called “curse of Ham” in Genesis. In a word, churchly resistance to slavery quickly melted away. By the time an infant United States of America proclaimed its independence, the great majority of Christian preachers here were solidly convinced that chattel slavery was God’s will. And our “one drop rule” for racial purity? Why, that’s directly linked to the religious “purity of blood” ( limpieza de sangre ) demanded by Catholic Spain. As for territorial conquest, the North American Protestants may have hated everything else about the Church of Rome, but they were more than happy to adopt the Doctrine of Discovery for their own purposes. More to the point, it is impossible to separate our mostly Protestant version of white Christian nationalism from the Catholic version of 15 th century Spain. Why? Because Protestant rigidity and Protestant zealotry in England and Holland—the wellsprings of our current torments—were directly forged in reaction to the very real mortal threat posed by Catholic Spain, and later by Catholic France, to the entire Protestant project in Northern Europe. From the reign of Henry VIII all the way through the so-called Glorious Revolution of 1689, it was touch and go for the Protestant cause in Britain. The success of Dutch Protestant resistance to mighty Spain was viewed by the English as a minor miracle, but it hardly eased their fears; rather, it inspired greater vigilance and even the importation of a Dutch monarch. So there we have it: white Christian nationalism emerged side-by-side with what historians consider the birth of the modern era in 1492. We’ve suffered the consequences ever since.

articles.title: UFCW Members Protect Local Election After Sham Merger Attempt
articles.author: Lisa Xu
articles.content: An insurgent slate is challenging the longtime incumbents in Local 8-Golden State, one of the largest locals in the United Food and Commercial Workers (UFCW), in what may be the local’s first competitive election in decades. And now, after protecting the election from a sham merger attempt that would have canceled the election, the battle is on. Ballots are set to be mailed on November 21. But when members first saw the election notice in the local’s newsletter, they discovered a big “but.” The notice stated that the election would not proceed if Local 8 merged with another union, the Staffing Agencies Federated Employees (SAFE), before the end of the year. Members said they had never heard about this possible merger, or SAFE, before reading about it in the final sentence of the election notice, mailed to members on October 16. What is SAFE? Publicly available information about the organization, which has multiple ties to Local 8 President Jacques Loveall, raised more questions than answers. Neither Local 8, the UFCW International union, nor SAFE has responded to inquiries about the merger. With the help of Essential Workers for Democracy , a UFCW reform organization focused on member education and union democracy, the insurgent slate urged the Department of Labor to investigate SAFE and the merger. After a federal investigator began to probe, the local told them the merger had been “postponed indefinitely.” A FAMILY AFFAIR Local 8 represents 23,000 workers in grocery, meatpacking, health care, and cannabis across northern California and the Central Valley. End to end, it would take 10 hours to drive the length of the local’s jurisdiction. The reform slate At What Cost is running on opening up negotiations to members and training stewards in every workplace. Wages for grocery workers have stagnated across California. A 2025 study sponsored by several other UFCW locals on understaffing at Kroger and Albertsons found a high degree of financial insecurity among their workers. “Grocery careers, once dignified, have been reduced to second jobs for most,” said Eric Marcuz, a veteran Safeway worker who is running for president on the At What Cost slate. The local has not had a competitive election in at least 40 years. Marcuz’s slate created a page to try to provide members more information about the merger, and sent a letter of complaint to Local 8, UFCW International, and the Department of Labor over what they saw as an effort to avoid a democratic election. The At What Cost slate is running against a slate of incumbents—the Solidarity Works Team — headed by Loveall, who has been president of Local 8 and its predecessor union, Local 588, since 2004. He took over the position from his father, Jack Loveall , who became president of Local 588 in 1984, after working in high-level positions for the UFCW International and one of its predecessor unions, the Retail Clerks, for many years. When the elder Loveall retired, he was one of the highest-paid union officers in the country, earning more than $567,000 in compensation a year, equivalent to over a million dollars today. “The Loveall family has led our union for decades,” said Marcuz. “Over that time they have consolidated power at the top and completely distanced themselves from the workers they claim to represent. While their wealth and wages have ballooned, the members have been left behind.” On his LinkedIn page, the younger Loveall describes himself as “Chief Executive Officer of trade organization (UFCW8.org).” He received $306,000 in total compensation from the local last year, plus another $20,000 salary as an International Vice President and $34,752 from his role as a trustee of the UFCW Vacation Compensation Trusts. Loveall is also the director and co-founder of Solidaritus, a for-profit health care company that Local 8 has purchased millions of dollars of shares in, as have other unions. ‘THAT’S THEIR MODE OF OPERATING’ Leaders of the local have used a merger to avoid a competitive election before. In 2006, a slate of reformers planned a challenge to the leadership of then-Local 588, including Loveall. But prior to the scheduled election, Local 588 merged with Local 1288 to form Local 8-Golden State, and elections were put off until 2008. Meanwhile, Doug Slaydon, a 25-year meat cutter and the reform slate’s candidate for union president, was fired from Safeway on the pretext of a customer complaint in 2006. The firing occurred a day after a 20-store campaign blitz by his slate, 588 Members for a Democratic Union. “That's their mode of operating,” Slaydon said, referring to the mergers. “That's how they got around my attempt at an election.” “Federal law is clear: local unions must hold officer elections at least every three years,” said Will Bloom, a professor at the CUNY School of Law and a board member of the Association for Union Democracy. “Any attempt to forestall an election through a sham merger, in an effort to quash dissent and make member participation more difficult, goes against the basic principles of union democracy law.” A REAL UNION? The proposed merger with SAFE immediately raised the eyebrows of members and the Department of Labor. It is not clear who SAFE represents, or whether it is even a union. On its website , SAFE calls itself a “labor-driven initiative committed to securing union inclusion and equitable treatment for workers employed through staffing agencies.” However, there are no union election filings by SAFE with the National Labor Relations Board, nor any other public documentation of where members are being organized. The organization’s website is filled with stock photos, rather than photos of actual members. An initial LM-1 form for SAFE was filed on February 9, 2026 by Patricia Schreiter, who appears to be a relative of Loveall, and has no other public connection to the labor movement. Schreiter was not listed on SAFE’s website as an officer, although the LM-1 form lists her as president. After members and a federal investigator from the Department of Labor began asking questions, the page listing SAFE’s officers and staff was removed from its site. As of early last week, the SAFE homepage stated the organization was “9,800 Strong and Growing,” but this figure has since been removed. A legislative update on the SAFE site from September 30 included a reference to union mergers as a strategy “to build a larger, stronger, more unified organization,” as “bigger unions win bigger protections”, but this language has also been removed. The SAFE website features dozens of articles about the SAFE Act, or SB 1032, a California state senate bill sponsored by Senator Eloise Reyes that would tighten regulatory standards for temporary staffing agencies and require them to buy workers’ compensation insurance. Loveall has been a vocal supporter of the bill via the UFCW Western States Council, the bill’s co-sponsor. However, an aide for Senator Reyes told Labor Notes that the SAFE union was not registered as a group in support of the bill, or one that they had personally interacted with. WEB OF CONNECTIONS There are a number of suggestive ties between SAFE and an organization called The PACT , which claims to be a 501(c)5 labor organization for temp workers. Until early last week SAFE’s organizing director was listed as Fernando Cisneros, whose LinkedIn profile states that he is also a full-time “Growth Leader” at The PACT. (Cisneros’s name disappeared when SAFE removed that section of its website.) The PACT has an arrangement with a company called Samuel Hale , which provides workers’ compensation insurance to the employers of temp workers and acts as a co-employer of those workers. “In addition to passing along savings to our customers, Samuel Hale also reinvests a percentage of every payroll dollar worked into a benefits fund managed by The PACT, a 501c5, exclusively focused on developing and administering new benefits to our growing 10,000+ member population,” Samuel Hale writes on its website. These workers appear to be mostly immigrant workers in sectors including warehouse work, food processing, and domestic services. As of earlier this week, SAFE’s website had a section called “Health Care & Retirement Benefits,” which stated that SAFE members will receive a defined benefit pension plan, as well as comprehensive medical coverage. These are both benefits which The PACT claims to offer to its employees. This section on the SAFE website, too, has since been removed. Samuel Hale and Local 8 appear to have a collective bargaining agreement, and seem to be utilizing California’s Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) carve-out, a state law that allows for workers’ compensation claims to be directly arbitrated between a union and employer, bypassing the state’s worker compensation board. A collective bargaining agreement must be in place in order to qualify for the carve-out. Loveall of Local 8 (then Local 588) appears to have signed a collective bargaining agreement in 2005 with Samuel Hale on behalf of The Professional and Commercial Trades Association (PACT), according to a video posted on the company’s Facebook page. In a 2025 workers’ comp appeal case, a Samuel Hale spokesperson said that the Samuel Hale employees are covered by a UFCW CBA and that The PACT is “a wing of the UFCW.” However, the details of this agreement are unclear and cannot be found online. The worker who filed the appeal also said that Local 8 was unable to provide “any information regarding alleged union membership,” even as Samuel Hale affirmed that union dues were being deducted from employee paychecks. Samuel Hale says that it can help employers cut workers’ comp claim costs by up to 50 percent, and boasts that it is the only entity covered by the California ADR carve-out that can extend the carve-out’s protection to other employers, thanks to its CBA with Local 8. In addition to the web of connections between SAFE, The PACT, Samuel Hale, and Local 8, SAFE’s articles of incorporation were filed July 17, 2025 by Ellen Anreder . Anreder is the CEO of Bleiweiss Communications , a major vendor for Local 8. Website metadata indicates that SAFE’s website was also created by Bleiweiss. Anreder and Loveall together serve on several non-profit boards that Local 8 has financial ties to, including CORPaTH , the Food and Drug Conference , the Loveall Foundation for Children , and All Trusts Cooperative (of which Anreder and Loveall are the only two board members), with a collective net assets of over $10 million. FUTURES AT STAKE In the UFCW, local union bylaws typically allow for elections to be called at any point in a six-month window preceding the end of a term, giving incumbents a powerful advantage, since challengers can't be sure when exactly they might need to take time off to collect nomination signatures or campaign to turn out the vote. What’s more, Local 8 has scheduled ballots to be mailed during the week of Thanksgiving, a universal blackout period for time off in the grocery retail sector. That’s exactly the week when candidates could most effectively campaign at worksites. The At What Cost slate notified the local union of their intent to run in August 2025, although reformers have been publicly agitating in the local since late 2024. But even talking about doing more to engage members has had repercussions. After Marcuz read Jane McAlevey’s organizing guide No Shortcuts , he brought up the possibility of opening up bargaining to his union rep. A few days later, he was removed from his position as steward, and was told that more “loyalty” was expected from him. Marcuz and his co-workers encountered similar resistance when they collected 300 petition signatures for Zoom access to union meetings, which are only held in-person at the union office in Roseville—a several-hour drive for many members of the local, which is spread out across 40 counties. The same happened when they organized bowling socials. During their campaign, union staff representatives have allegedly told members that it’s illegal to wear At What Cost buttons or to provide contact information to the slate. At a Safeway store in Turlock, a rep physically pulled a member away from speaking to Marcuz. “Workers face exploitation through contract violations, wage theft, and unsafe staffing and working conditions,” Marcuz said. “We could organize against these issues, but our leadership seems more interested in collaborating with the corporations creating these conditions than with the members who pay their salaries.” In early November, members of the slate will be working to collect 443 petition signatures—2 percent of active members—to get on the ballot and force the first competitive election in memory.

articles.title: Who’s Afraid of Gen Z Socialism?
articles.author: Elias Koenig
articles.content: What’s on the mind of the ruling class these days? If the pages of The Economist are a reliable indicator, it’s the specter of “ Gen Z socialism ”: the rising support among young people for taxing billionaires, socializing the economy, and stopping the genocide in Gaza, as evidenced by the popularity of politicians like New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, England’s Green Party leader Zack Polanski, or French presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Earlier this summer, the magazine dedicated a whole issue to “fighting back” against this “threat to prosperity,” calling on fellow free-market liberals to “stop apologizing” and level a “punchier defense of capitalism.” The rage bait worked: the magazine’s mailbox was flooded with critical responses, a selection of which it later published in a section titled “Were we too quick to attack Gen Z socialism?” The real pushback, however, has come from the streets. Around the world, Gen Z–led mass movements are decrying the rising cost of living and political corruption, as well as calling for better education, health care, and environmental protections. India is a case in point: on the very day that The Economist ’s editorial was published, tens of thousands of angry young protesters flooded New Delhi, engaging in street battles with a disoriented and violent local police force and bringing the heart of the Indian capital to a standstill. The protests had been sparked by remarks made by Indian Chief Justice Surya Kant, who had compared unemployed young people to “cockroaches” and “parasites” during a Supreme Court hearing. Initially focused on educational accountability, the movement has since broadened its platform to include demands for electoral and economic reforms. India’s Cockroach protests are only the latest in a series of Gen Z uprisings that were initially largely concentrated in Asia and Africa. In Nepal , Madagascar , Bangladesh , and Sri Lanka , student movements toppled entire governments. Elsewhere protests were brutally repressed or even culminated in a bloody civil war, as in Myanmar . This fall has seen a spillover of youth-led mass mobilizations into various European countries. In France, Belgium, and Italy, high school students have been spearheading massive protests against educational austerity; in Spain and Portugal, young people are leading demonstrations against soaring housing costs ; Albania’s “ Flamingo Revolution ” is calling for the resignation of the prime minister over ecologically and socially harmful tourism development, including a controversial resort backed by Jared Kushner, son-in-law of US President Donald Trump; and in Serbia a new Student List has just celebrated a historic victory, winning an absolute majority in Sunday’s parliamentary elections after two years of youth-led anti-corruption and anti-mining protests. But is this really all about generational difference? How Not to Think About Generations The label “Gen Z” is hardly sufficient to describe such a diverse range of social movements. In many cases, it’s a cliché imposed from the outside by pundits with little understanding of local dynamics. At the same time, generation has undoubtedly become one of the key vectors along which movements organize and identify themselves, from Madagascar’s “ Gen Z Mada ” and Morocco’s “ Gen Z 212 ” to Germany’s “ Gen Z regelt .” “You messed with the wrong generation!” the rallying cry of Myanmar’s 2021 civil disobedience movement, has become a popular motto across the region. In France, the slogan “Génération 6–7 refait Mai 68" (Generation 6–7 is doing May ’68 all over again) has gone viral . How should socialists relate to such generation-based movements? Unlike class, race, or gender, generation is not a category that has traditionally been at the heart of socialist politics. Generational designations like “boomers,” “Gen X,” “millennials,” or “Gen Z” are not the product of Marxist theory but of predominantly US business consultants, pollsters, and think tanks like the Pew Research Center . Since the 1960s, US marketing corporations have built a profitable industry around studying the attitudes and preferences of supposed generational cohorts. It’s worth highlighting the sheer absurdity of the generational thinking that is at the heart of this corporate “science.” Its most influential articulation remains that of William Strauss and Neil Howe, two former congressional staffers, who mapped out their “theory” over a series of books, including Generations (1991) and The Fourth Turning (1997). Strauss and Howe argue that human history progresses in continuous eighty-to-one-hundred-year cycles. Each cycle corresponds to roughly one long human lifespan and can be broken down into four seasons (“turnings”), which always occur in the exact same sequence: First comes a high, a period of constant expansion. Next comes an awakening, a time of spiritual exploration and rebellion. Then comes an unraveling, in which individualism triumphs over crumbling institutions. Last comes a crisis — the fourth turning — when society passes through a great and perilous gate in history. Every period corresponds to one of four generational archetypes, which, in turn, give rise to one another by way of a specific parenting style: the prophet, the nomad, the hero, and the artist. According to Strauss and Howe, the recurrence of these different child-rearing styles can explain nearly everything: developments in popular culture, workplace dynamics, economic crises, wars, and all other major events in US history since 1584. Their esoteric musings are loved by political elites of all stripes. Steve Bannon has described The Fourth Turning as “central to his worldview” and based his 2010 documentary “Generation Zero” on its arguments. During his time as Donald Trump’s top aide, Bannon reportedly kept an annotated copy of the book on his shelf. Al Gore, Strauss’s Harvard classmate, called Generations “the most stimulating and politically relevant book on American history that I have ever read” and sent a copy of the book to every single member of Congress. Bill Clinton, in turn, is said to have been influenced by the book in his decision to choose fellow baby boomer Gore as a running mate for the 1992 presidential race. Unsurprisingly, many thinkers on the Left have been suspicious of generational discourse. Commenting on last year’s Gen Z uprisings, Vincent Bevins argues : “For over a century, it has been young people who are most likely to take to the streets and take risks. Claiming that an uprising will be ‘led by Generation Z’ amounts to little more than saying that it will happen in 2025. . . . I think the generational framework is a symptom of intellectual poverty.” In the same vein, Adolph Reed Jr warns : The generational frame of reference is a product of pollsters and consultants who have a political service to sell that is an alternative to organizing durable constituencies around issues, programs, and political vision — the approach through which political movements actually take shape. . . . This strategy will never help us advance a broadly egalitarian agenda. Capitalism’s Generational Rift Bevins, Reed, and many others are right to criticize the shallowness of liberal generation-based frameworks. Talk of generations often obscures what is at the heart of the present crisis: capitalism and its system of class and market rule. Yet if the current wave of uprisings illustrates anything, it is that many young people do experience the crises of our time in explicitly generational terms. Globally, more than two billion people belong to Gen Z, i.e., those born between 1997 and 2012, making it the largest generation ever born. Combined with the similarly large Gen Alpha, they make up almost half of the global population. Capitalism has been struggling to integrate this massive new cohort of workers into a faltering world economy. Nine out of ten young workers in low- and lower-middle-income countries (which host the majority of the Gen Z population) are employed informally and without protections. Youth unemployment has also been on the rise . The US-Israeli war of aggression against Iran has only exacerbated this situation, driving up inflation and causing global shortages in oil, gas, fertilizers, and petrochemicals. While Gen Z protests in the Global South have largely focused on anti-corruption demands, protests in Europe have centered on austerity and the cost-of-living crisis. Both issues concern key strategies employed by the ruling class in response to the deepening structural crisis of the global economy: on the one hand, the fusion of political and economic power and the emergence of a new state capitalism , which has led to new forms of profiteering and corruption; on the other hand, the dismantling of the welfare state and the expansion of rentier capitalism in the imperial core. Other common themes in Gen Z protests include rising rents, military conscription, climate breakdown, and anxiety over the impact of artificial intelligence — all of which are symptoms of the crisis of capitalism that disproportionately affect young people. In this sense, the current crisis has a distinctly generational dimension. As political theorist and historian Timothy Mitchell argues in his new book The Alibi of Capital , this is no accident. According to Mitchell, intergenerational injustice is a fundamental feature of capitalism, “a form of life built on taking livelihoods from the future.” As political economist Keir Milburn argues in his book Generation Left , the shared experience of historical events such as pandemics or financial crises can forge what he calls “political generations” — generational units that rally around a shared interpretation of the events witnessed, as well as a shared collective response to them. Milburn notes that not everyone automatically becomes part of the same “political generation.” Within a certain age group, there may very well be different responses to the same conjuncture, which would then form different “generational units.” Importantly, this leaves room to account for different class positions and interests that exist even within the same age group, and that ought to remain central to any understanding of how capitalism operates. Many Gen Z protesters recognize this interplay of class and generation. A defining element of the recent uprisings has been class hatred against “nepo babies,” the children of the politicians and other elites who are flaunting their wealth online. In Nepal, viral photos of a provincial minister’s son showing an enormous pile of gift boxes from luxury brands like Louis Vuitton, Gucci, and Cartier fanned the flames of popular anger. In the Philippines, netizens began conducting so-called lifestyle checks on Reddit , scrutinizing the consumption practices of popular politicians and their family members in light of their declared income. In Germany, high school students striking against military conscription have chosen the motto “The rich want war — the youth, a future.” Seizing the Moment It’s not just The Economist and its acolytes who are at a loss over such outbursts of generational rage. The reaction of the ruling class at large reveals an utter lack of both economic literacy and political imagination. While politicians like Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar, Poland’s Donald Tusk, and Donald Trump have echoed far-right talking points blaming mass migration for the unrest, EU legislators are now investigating the alleged role of Russian, Algerian, and Iranian foreign interference. Similar rhetoric can be observed in India, where Narendra Modi’s government has sought to cast Gen Z protests as foreign-funded . Meanwhile, liberal reporting often focuses on the role of social media and various pop culture references in the protests, from the straw-hat pirate flags of the popular Japanese anime One Piece to the three-finger salute inspired by The Hunger Games . Yet if there is anything new about this protest wave, it is not the occurrence of leaderless mass demonstrations, political violence, or the use of social media as a mobilizing tool (the 2010s provide ample material to study any of them), but the extent to which generation has been globalized as a political identity. Somehow groups as diverse as young Burmese guerrillas, Indonesian delivery riders, and French high school students have all come to think of themselves as part of a political subject called “Gen Z,” as if this were the most natural thing in the world. While social media platforms like Discord and TikTok have helped circulate generational discourse originating in the United States, the ease with which it has caught on can only be explained with reference to the fundamental political and economic challenges facing young people across the world: economic precarity, ecological breakdown, and the escalation of imperial violence. The ruling class is scared of Gen Z socialism because it has no answer to these challenges. Socialists are taking note. In France, Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s party La France Insoumise (LFI) has thrown its weight behind the youth uprising. Videos of Bally Bagayoko, the LFI mayor of Saint-Denis, shielding student protesters from riot police have since gone viral around the world. In India, communist student unions have been an integral part of the Cockroach mobilizations since the early days of the movement. That early involvement is now paying off, with Neha Bora , the eloquent and defiant president of the Marxist-Leninist All India Students’ Association (AISA), becoming the face of the latest round of mobilizations. Who knows which country will be next? This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: Alberta’s Separation Ballot Ended With a Whimper
articles.author: Gerard Di Trolio
articles.content: No country treats referendums as less definitive than Canada. Two sovereignty referendums in Quebec have not totally put to bed the independence question in la belle province , and in spite of declining referendum support, the new Parti Québécois government is promising a third when Donald Trump leaves office. Voters rejected a set of constitutional amendments known as the Charlottetown Accord in 1992, but constitutional issues continue to fester with no federal government willing to touch them. This history matters when considering Alberta’s recent referendum. On the surface, the repudiation of Albertan independence was decisive, with 75.05 percent voting for Alberta to remain a province of Canada instead of beginning the legal process toward a binding referendum on separation. But voters also answered nine other questions, covering immigration, proof of citizenship to vote, and constitutional reform. The four immigration questions passed with between 52 and 54 percent. The proposal to require proof of citizenship to vote also passed, with about 58 percent. Even with Alberta staying, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith could face a political reckoning reminiscent of UK Prime Minister David Cameron’s after Brexit. To appease Euroskeptics in his party, Cameron called the referendum, campaigned to stay in the European Union, and resigned when voters chose to leave. Both leaders gave their parties’ right wings a vote on a demand they hoped to contain. Cameron’s experience shows how such a vote can spiral out of control, empowering the very forces a leader hopes to manage and having lasting political effects long after the votes are counted. Smith says she voted to keep Alberta in Canada, but a majority of Albertans think she wants the province to leave. An Abacus poll conducted in February, months before the referendum, found that 53 percent thought she would vote to separate. A June Ipsos poll found that about 40 percent of her United Conservative Party (UCP) voter base backed separation, while 50 percent preferred to remain. Calgary, traditionally more conservative than Edmonton, the provincial capital, voted 85 to 15 to keep Alberta in Canada. Smith now faces pressure from two directions. Calgary remains essential for the UCP’s political fortunes, but the party recently lost the Calgary-Shaw by-election to the left-wing New Democratic Party (NDP). Some UCP constituency associations are pushing for a leadership review at the party’s general meeting this November. The UCP may yet turn on itself, even as the NDP’s political fortunes continue to rise. A Mainstreet poll published right before the referendum had the two parties tied in voting intention, despite NDP leader Naheed Nenshi’s relatively low approval rating . Smith has other weapons that may save her. Voter approval for the four immigration-related proposals gives her an opening to press Ottawa for greater provincial control over immigration. High oil prices are also helping Alberta’s economy grow faster than the Canadian average. Still, the referendum has left Smith caught between the separatist sentiment within her own party and the clear preference among Albertans to remain in Canada. It may mark the beginning of political headwinds for Smith — and even possibly for the UCP. A Very Canadian Polycrisis The results on immigration should come as little surprise. Support for immigration in Canada has plummeted since the COVID-19 pandemic. Yet Canada needs immigration to sustain economic growth, particularly as the country’s population ages and labor force participation declines. At the same time, the labor market is weakening. After some gains earlier in the year, Canada had lost about 41,000 jobs by September, with losses concentrated among young workers . This labor market weakness is occurring as the country attempts to reorient its economy away from the United States. Statistics Canada has yet to find clear evidence of artificial-intelligence-related employment reduction, but the prospect is on the minds of many workers. A survey of US economists found little expectation of a job apocalypse, but many anticipate difficult sectoral transitions and downward pressure on wages for workers with higher education. If job prospects remain weak, the Left must tread carefully. Alberta is the clearest expression of Canada’s resource-dependent economy. Mark Carney has doubled down on expanding resource exports, without an extensive industrial policy to promote domestic processing. Meanwhile, the US-Israeli war on Iran is accelerating the transition away from fossil fuels, even as prices are soaring. In time, the shock caused by the war may hasten demand destruction, as costs and supply insecurity push consumers and governments toward alternatives. In this scenario, because of the high cost of oil sands extraction, the province will be hit hard . This is about more than economics. In Canada, natural resources, especially fossil fuels, have become a culture war flash point. Despite jobs in the Alberta oil sector being automated away , claims that environmentalists want to take jobs away from hardworking Albertans still abound. Canada once organized much of its political economy around manufacturing in Ontario and Quebec, and this history is now invoked to express regional grievances. Today resource dependence means oil booms can strengthen the Canadian dollar at the expense of industry in Eastern Canada. Escaping from boom-and-bust cycles, regional grievances, and anxieties about labor markets and immigration will require skillful political leadership. It will also require an economic strategy focused on jobs, capable of delivering affordable necessities, including clean energy and housing, as Canada builds a less resource-dependent economy — an economy that moves away from its role as “hewer of wood and drawer of water.” Until then, Alberta’s contradictions will shape the country one way or another. articles.title: AOC 2028: A Historic Opportunity to Build the Socialist Movement
articles.author: Elliot Lewis and James Hernández
articles.content: Why DSA Members Should Support AOC 2028 Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is a DSA member and a champion of popular reforms like Medicare for All, blocking all military aid to Israel, the PRO Act, and a Green New Deal. She is also the only potential democratic socialist contender for President in 2028. Bernie Sanders’ 2016 and 2020 Presidential campaigns caused DSA to grow enormously. We saw the importance of having a left-wing candidate contest the Presidency, to spread socialist ideas and jump-start an opportunity for organizing on a big scale. Conversely we saw how demobilizing it was in 2024 to have no alternative to the centrist candidate that had been handed the nomination. Electing a democratic socialist President would give us an unprecedented opportunity to build the labor movement and the Left through the bully pulpit of executive office, and the potential to organize for transformative reforms. We recognize that this is far from a guaranteed result but we also know that even the process of running opens up opportunities to expand the political imagination of the public. The highly successful DSA for Bernie campaigns also show the importance of laying the groundwork for a national Presidential campaign as early as possible, even before a candidate announces they are running. DSA members should encourage AOC to run and begin planning now how to make the most of her campaign, to grow the socialist movement. Two vehicles that we should plan in advance are Students for AOC and Labor For AOC. Student Organizing An AOC Presidential run could serve to organize young people and students at a rate never seen before. If YDSA leads youth organizing for AOC, we can connect young people to the Workers Deserve More program and long-term organizing as workers, tenants, and students. In 2025, YDSA kicked off the year with just over 1,800 DSA members. This year, YDSA membership has nearly tripled. First, the campaign to elect Zohran Mamdani energized young people across the country. Students tabled with Zohran cutouts, using his campaign to connect with other students about transformative demands on our campuses. Then, with the several high-profile federal races won this year by DSAers, YDSA has grown to more than 5,000 members, and is now using its campaign for Sanctuary Campuses to organize them for the long haul. YDSA should adopt support for AOC’s campaign as the national priority campaign for the 2027-2028 term. This would mean national YDSA creating resources and mentoring chapters. An AOC Presidential campaign would allow YDSA to do something we’ve been trying to experiment with for a long time – running a coherent national campaign with shared tactics. YDSAers campaigning for AOC would unify not only around her platform but around the Workers Deserve More program, using it to expose young people to socialist politics and organize them into the student and labor movements for the future. An AOC 2028 campaign would be different from the other national campaigns YDSA has adopted in the past, because it would provide a popular shared goal and common organizing framework across the country. This campaign would allow us to connect with working class students across departments, social circles, identities, and interest groups to build unity on our campuses. This would allow us to expand our base into the areas of campus that may otherwise be inaccessible to young socialists. Labor for AOC Socialist labor activists should begin planning with like-minded coworkers now on how to build Labor for AOC efforts in their unions as soon as she announces, for three reasons: 1) early efforts will be crucial in cohering portions of the labor movement behind AOC, 2) engagement of union members in an AOC campaign can stimulate internal and external union organizing beyond the campaign, and 3) it’s an opportunity to bridge the labor movement and the socialist movement. In 2016 and 2020, union activists built a national Labor for Bernie group that organized union members to vote for Bernie in the early primaries and caucuses. Labor for AOC could produce materials and trainings to help rank-and-filers bring their coworkers to canvasses for AOC and organize to secure their unions’ endorsement. The efforts of some union activists in New York City around Zohran’s 2025 mayoral campaign illustrate these tactics. Rank-and-file union activists in AFSCME’s city workers union, District Council 37, organized enough members to persuade the leadership to endorse Zohran second in the ranked-choice primary. Educators for Zohran in the teachers union (UFT) were able to stop the union from endorsing against Zohran in the primary. After UFT endorsed Zohran in the general election, these rank-and-file educators made the endorsement carry weight by doing their own flyering and phonebanking turnout for official UFT for Zohran canvasses. If union activists organized at a larger scale nationally, they could bring their unions into the AOC campaign coalition early on, bolstering her campaign and engaging millions of union workers in democratic socialist politics. Union members would be well positioned to talk union to workers they encounter while canvassing. Non-union workers reached through Labor for AOC tabling and canvassing could be connected to resources like EWOC and other worker organizer trainings to get them interested in union drives. Finally, by giving union activists a framework to talk about socialist politics in a relevant and clear way, the Labor for AOC campaign could help bring thousands more union activists into the socialist movement. It can be hard in workplace organizing to connect specific workplace struggles with the need to move society from capitalism to socialism. A democratic socialist Presidential campaign would help bridge that gap by bringing discussions about socialism onto the national political stage, grounded in reform demands that matter to unionists, like the PRO Act, Medicare for All, and housing for all. A campaign structure gives us a framework of escalating asks to engage coworkers in politics, like coming to a Labor for AOC canvass, going to AOC-related DSA events, and joining DSA. Ready Day One An AOC 2028 Presidential campaign is a historic opportunity for democratic socialists to engage millions of people in our politics. DSA members should make the most of this possibility now by moving the organization to begin strategizing around an AOC 2028 campaign. Let’s be prepared on the day it launches. articles.title: Lula’s Surprise Victory Is a Beam of Hope in a Dark World
articles.author: Hugo Albuquerque
articles.content: Following a stunning, inspiring turnaround driven by mass mobilization of the Brazilian people, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won his fourth presidential election. This achievement marks an unprecedented shift in Brazilian political history: never before has a candidate who trailed in the first round managed to come back and win. The election — which pitted Lula against Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is currently imprisoned for an attempted coup d’état following his defeat in the 2022 elections — was marked by obscene interference from the Trump administration, with Big Tech companies like Meta acting shamelessly in favor of the far right. All this in a context where other interventions in the region by Trump were successful, leading to the election of far-right presidents — most notably in Colombia — which created the sense of an invincible Trumpist wave across Latin America. Defeated by about two million votes on October 4, Lula gained more than ten million new votes on October 25, while Flávio Bolsonaro received just over three and a half million more than in the first round. Lula increased his vote share in virtually every Brazilian municipality after having been written off just three weeks ago. What changed in such a short time provides a lesson for socialists the world over. How a Victory Is Built While pro-Lula demonstrations began immediately after the defeat in the first round, driven largely by student organizations, the Workers’ Party campaign sought to connect with a new generation on the left wing. At the same time, it triggered a genuine earthquake in the party’s communication strategy, brought about by the arrival of Congressman André Janones, recently reelected as a candidate for the center-left party Rede. Lula, who is eighty, invited an entirely new generation of newly elected congresspeople to Brasília immediately following the first round of voting. Despite the growth of the far right at the expense of the traditional right and center in the legislative elections, held concurrently with the first round of the presidential race, the Left made gains in the National Congress, bringing in young figures who are adept at social media and communication and who brought fresh energy to the campaign. Among these rising stars are twenty-one-year-old representative Ana Elisa — hailing from Minas Gerais, Brazil’s quintessential swing state; Erika Hilton, a trans woman reelected with a record number of votes; Jones Manoel, a communist from Pernambuco (Lula’s home state); and Guilherme Cortez, a representative who identifies as a twink. They all represent a generation of young people with millions of Gen Z fans in Brazil; they are social media stars, despite the platform algorithms favoring right-wing content. But the campaign’s most notable figure was forty-two-year-old Janones, who created a WhatsApp group dubbed Exército de Lula (Lula’s Army) that grew to over ten million followers, through which he carried out organized and disciplined agitation and propaganda. Nearly one in every ten Brazilian voters joined a single group in just three weeks. Janones is often snubbed by the old intellectual left-wing elite, yet he has always been popular with the masses. Now he has become a true celebrity. Working from the assumption that Meta’s algorithm was biased against the Left, Janones orchestrated major social media campaigns, such as encouraging Lula’s supporters to post Instagram photos of themselves wearing the Brazilian national soccer team jersey, a garment once a symbol of unity but subsequently co-opted by the far right. This action was joined by countless Lula supporters and made a major splash on social media one day before the failed demonstration organized by Flávio Bolsonaro on Avenida Paulista, a vital hub in the city of São Paulo. The strategy was a success, with Janones playfully repurposing the far right’s military vocabulary, referring to his followers in Lula’s Army as “soldiers.” Beyond the algorithms, this move by Janones subverted the semiotics of recent years, during which the Bolsonaro family mobilized its vast base using military terminology — a natural enough approach, given that Bolsonaro and many of his key behind-the-scenes figures are or once were military men. The Brazilian Far Right Cornered for the First Time Even after its defeat in 2022, the far right remained a powerful force on social media, driven by a combination of effective communication and preferential treatment by the platforms’ parent companies. During the Lula administration, posts by pro-Bolsonaro Congressman Nikolas Ferreira garnered higher engagement than those of global pop stars. This was used to wage a dirty yet highly effective opposition campaign against the third Lula administration. While Lula appeared mired in a series of political missteps upon his heroic return to the presidency in 2022, leading a complex Broad Front coalition, his opponents seemed unbeatable on social media and effectively connected with the Brazilian people. Obviously, the criticisms from the far right had little to do with the problems facing Lula’s third administration; rather, Bolsonaro allies leveraged the government’s relative unpopularity to advance their own agenda of dismantling Brazilian democracy. After defeating Bolsonaro in 2022, a victory that echoed his own political comeback from his time as president in the 2000s, Lula seemed trapped in a Groundhog Day scenario, where every government crisis was amplified by mass agitation from the far right. Curiously, this state of stagnation only came to an end in the last three weeks. Janones’s strategy brought fresh air, pulling millions of activists out of a potentially deadly depression, given the imminent return of fascism, as veteran journalist Luiz Carlos Azenha stated . Janones’s insane twenty-four-hour live stream before the elections was preceded by a live stream with millions of views featuring testimonials from many Brazilian artists, showcasing perhaps the very best of Lula and Brazil. From that point on, the Right lost its comfortable monopoly on communication. Lula has once again reached the masses, for the first time since returning to the presidency. But this fourth term must entail governing in a different way. It will require an approach closer to his first two terms, in which Lula was able to set the terms of debate within the country, yet with a need for more intensive dialogue and action with the masses of Brazilians who delivered this election for him. All of this is taking place in a world that is, quite literally, on fire. The economy will be a problem, and Lula will have to confront a bourgeoisie that desires a more savage capitalism than anything seen before, even in Brazil. For those who saw Flávio Bolsonaro acting as if he were already president on October 25, Lula’s surprise victory was a historic relief. For those who have lived through the last few weeks in Brazil — attending massive demonstrations, unprecedented in the country’s electoral history, and growing furious at every debate between Lula and Flávio, as well as at the cruel and boundless arrogance of the right-wing leader — the operative word is, finally, hope.
